patristic_citations: Origen (Commentary on Matthew 13.7, c. 245 AD) — discusses demonic deliverance and explicitly treats the fasting mandate.
St. John Chrysostom (Homily 57 on Matthew, c. 390 AD) — 'He that fasteth is light and winged, and prayeth with wakefulness...'
St. Hilary of Poitiers (Commentary on Matthew, 4th c.)
St. Augustine (De Agone Christiano 32, c. 396 AD) — expounds on the union of bodily fasting with prayer against principalities.

textual_criticism.critical_theory: Modern critical editors (Westcott-Hort, Bruce Metzger) assume Matthew 17:21 was an intentional or accidental harmonization by Byzantine scribes borrowing from Mark 9:29. Because the 4th-century uncials Sinaiticus and Vaticanus omit it, modern critical editions drop it.
textual_criticism.traditional_catholic_defense: Attestation in the bilingual Western text (Codex Bezae D) and the Old Latin tradition demonstrates the verse existed across both Greek and Latin branches long before Sinaiticus and Vaticanus were penned. St. Jerome included it in the Latin Vulgate, which the Council of Trent declared authentic. Alexandrian ascetic scribes often practiced homeoteleuton or omission when texts overlapped with other Synoptic records.
textual_criticism.theological_impact: Directly impacts the theology of asceticism, penance, and bodily mortification. In modern Protestant circles where fasting is minimized (as in the Discord screenshot: 'bro told me we dont need to fast because jesus already fasted'), the omission reinforces an antinomian or anti-ascetical stance by excising Christ's explicit rule for high-order spiritual warfare.
